617.title: Whom he sees not (1 John 4:20)
617.hook: how can you love God whom you don't see if you don't love your brother
617.tomorrow: keep yourselves in the love of God
617.howItsDone: At Mass, after the Lord's Prayer and before Communion, Catholics may exchange a sign of peace with the people around them, and the Church teaches that love of God and love of neighbor are inseparable.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a child at the edge of the pool, and perfect charity. Your line was love casts out fear. What first step did love get you to take? Day six hundred seventeen.

In Dostoevsky's novel The Brothers Karamazov, the old monk Zosima tells about a doctor who once admitted something embarrassing. The more he loved humanity in general, the doctor said, the less he loved actual people in particular. In his dreams he'd gladly die for the human race. But put him in a room with one real person for a day, and he couldn't stand the way they blew their nose or how slowly they ate. Most of us have met that doctor. Some mornings he's in the mirror. John, near the end of his first letter, catches the same trick and turns it toward God.
screen: `DOSTOEVSKY'S DOCTOR.` → `HUMANITY, YES. PEOPLE, NO.` → `JOHN TURNS IT TOWARD GOD.`

segments.voice: John has just said that God is love and that love casts out fear. Then he brings it down to earth with a thud. The Douay-Rheims: "If any man say, I love God, and hateth his brother; he is a liar. For he that loveth not his brother, whom he seeth, how can he love God, whom he seeth not?" Liar is a strong word, and John means it. Not mistaken, not still growing: lying. Because love for God can stay very safe. God doesn't interrupt you, borrow your car, or chew loudly. Earlier in this same chapter John says that no one has ever seen God. So where does love for the unseen God get tested? On the seen. The coworker. The brother-in-law. The roommate. John's logic runs from the easier to the harder. If you can't manage the one in front of you, whose face you know, what makes you think you're managing the one you've never seen? And right after, he spells out the commandment: whoever loves God must love his brother also. The two loves aren't rivals. They're one love, facing two directions. Catholics act this out at every Mass. Just before Communion, before receiving the Lord they cannot see, people turn to whoever happens to be next to them and offer a sign of peace. A handshake, a nod, sometimes to a stranger, sometimes to the family member they were arguing with in the car. Jesus said something like it: if you remember at the altar that your brother has something against you, go first and be reconciled, then come back and offer your gift.
screen: `IF ANY MAN SAY, I LOVE GOD...` · `NO ONE HAS EVER SEEN GOD.` · `ONE LOVE, FACING TWO WAYS.` · `THE SIGN OF PEACE BEFORE COMMUNION.` · then, large: `WHOM HE SEETH, AND WHOM HE SEETH NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love the person nearest you. Sit comfortably and breathe. Think of the person physically closest to your life right now, the one you'll see today: in your home, at the next desk, across the hall. Not the easiest person. Just the nearest. Picture their face, including the things about them that wear on you. Breathe through that. Then think of one small way to love them today: a kind word, patience with a habit, a cup of tea, listening all the way to the end of a story. If you pray, you can hold them before God by name. If you don't, just look at them kindly in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Whom he sees not. First John four: love for the God no one has seen is tested on the brother and sister we can see. Today's word.
Your line: love the one you see. Today, do the small loving thing for the nearest person, especially if they're not the easiest. Day six hundred seventeen.

618.title: Keep yourselves in the love of God (Jude 20–25)
618.hook: Jude ends with a glorious blessing to him who can keep you from falling
618.howItsDone: Catholics pray doxologies many times a day: the Glory Be after psalms and at each decade of the rosary, and at Mass the great doxology that ends the Eucharistic Prayer, to which the people answer Amen; Saint Jude is also invoked in desperate situations.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the God whom no one sees and the brother whom we do. Your line was love the one you see. How did the nearest person get loved? Day six hundred eighteen.

Some letters are easy to skip. The letter of Jude is a single page, tucked in just before the last book of the Bible, and most of it is a fierce warning about false teachers, with strange references to angels and old stories. People flip past it on their way to the Apocalypse. But the person who wrote it had something else to say before he signed off. He ends with a blessing that still gets prayed today, and it's the last stop on our long road through the letters.
screen: `A SINGLE PAGE, EASY TO SKIP.` → `WARNINGS, ANGELS, OLD STORIES.` → `THEN A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Jude introduces himself as the servant of Jesus Christ and the brother of James. Catholic tradition has long identified him with the apostle Jude, also called Thaddeus, whom Catholic tradition honors as a patron of desperate causes. Scholars discuss who exactly he was. Near the end, he turns from the danger to his readers, and gives them three things to do. Build yourselves up on your faith. Pray in the Holy Spirit. And, in the Douay-Rheims: "Keep yourselves in the love of God." It is a picture of staying put, inside a love that is already there, the way you stay near a fire on a cold night. Then he adds: be merciful to those who doubt, and pull others out of the fire. And then, the blessing. In the Douay-Rheims it begins: "Now to him who is able to preserve you without sin, and to present you spotless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy." The King James puts it as keep you from falling. Look at the shape of that. Jude has just told his readers to keep themselves in God's love. Then he gives the glory to the one who is able to keep them. Both are true at once. A blessing like this, one that ends a letter by giving glory to God, has a name: doxology, from the Greek doxa, glory, and logos, word. A word of glory. Catholics pray doxologies often: the Glory Be at the end of each decade of the rosary, and at Mass, the great one at the end of the Eucharistic Prayer, when the priest lifts the host and chalice and the people answer, Amen.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray Jude's blessing over someone. Sit comfortably and breathe. Bring to mind someone you're worried about, someone who seems close to falling: a friend struggling with faith, a teenager, someone tired of trying. Picture them clearly. If you pray, you can slowly say the start of Jude's blessing for them: now to him who is able to preserve you without sin, and to present you spotless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy. Then rest, and give the glory where Jude gives it. If you don't pray, just hold them in mind and wish them steady footing. The bell holds the time.
Doxology. A word of glory to God, like the blessing that ends Jude's letter. Today's word.

619.title: Reading the Apocalypse
619.hook: apocalypse means unveiling: a letter of hope to churches under pressure
619.howItsDone: Catholics hear the Apocalypse at Mass, especially in the Easter season and in the last weeks of the Church year, and its hymns run through the Liturgy of the Hours; the Church reads it as a book of hope in Christ's victory rather than a timetable for the end.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the end of the letters, and Jude's doxology. Your line was able to keep you. Who did you send a few words to? Day six hundred nineteen.

Say the word apocalypse to most people and they picture the end of the world: burning cities, empty highways, a zombie movie. Hollywood has made sure of that. Now go back to the date tradition gives, near the end of the first century. You're a small group of Christians in a city in what is now western Turkey. You meet in someone's house. The empire around you expects everyone to honor the emperor, and some of your people have paid for refusing. One Sunday a letter arrives from a man named John, who is on an island called Patmos. It's full of trumpets, beasts, a dragon and a city of gold. It's addressed to you.
screen: `APOCALYPSE: THE MOVIE VERSION.` → `A HOUSE CHURCH IN ASIA.` → `A LETTER FROM PATMOS.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Apocalypse is the book's first word in Greek, apokalypsis: an uncovering, the veil pulled off. It isn't destruction. It's unveiling. That's why some Bibles call the book Revelation, and the Douay-Rheims calls it the Apocalypse. Same word. Its very first line says it's the revelation of Jesus Christ, shown to his servant John. So what's being unveiled? Not mainly a timetable. Mostly, it's what's really going on behind what you can see. On the surface, Rome looks invincible and the little churches look finished. Pull back the curtain, and there's a throne in heaven, a Lamb who was slain and stands alive, and a worship that never stops. It's a letter of hope to churches under pressure. Second, it's a particular kind of writing, like parts of the book of Daniel: dreams, visions, numbers and creatures that stand for something. Readers have long taken seven as a sign of completeness. A beast isn't a zoology report. And then a promise in its opening lines: "Blessed is he, that readeth and heareth the words of this prophecy." A book meant to be read aloud, in church, to people who listen. Christians read the Apocalypse in different ways. Some read it as history told in advance, some as mostly about the first century, some as symbols for every age. Catholic teaching reads it on more than one level at once: a word to those first churches, a word to the Church in every time, and a hope for the end, when Christ comes again. The Church doesn't hand out a calendar of the last days. What it hands out is the book itself, read at Mass in the Easter season and as the Church year closes.
screen: `APOKALYPSIS: PULLING OFF THE VEIL.` · `WHAT'S REALLY GOING ON.` · `VISIONS, NUMBERS, CREATURES.` · `READ ALOUD, ON MORE THAN ONE LEVEL.` · then, large: `AN UNVEILING, NOT AN ENDING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: read chapter one once. If you have a Bible or an app nearby, open to the last book, the Apocalypse or Revelation, and read the first chapter slowly, as much as the bell allows. Read it aloud if you can, softly, the way it was first heard. Don't try to decode anything. Just notice what stays with you: a color, a sound, a voice like many waters, a right hand laid on someone afraid. If you don't have the text, sit quietly and picture that house church listening to it for the first time. If you pray, you can ask to see what's behind the veil. The bell holds the time.
Apocalypse. From the Greek for unveiling: pulling the cover off what's really going on. The last book of the Bible. Today's word.
Your line: an unveiling. Today, when something looks hopeless on the surface, ask what might be going on behind it. We're in the last book now, for thirteen days. Day six hundred nineteen.

620.title: Alpha and Omega (Apocalypse 1:8–18)
620.hook: John on Patmos sees the living one; the letters are cut into the Easter candle
620.howItsDone: At the Easter Vigil, the priest marks the new paschal candle with a cross, the letters alpha and omega and the numerals of the year, and may insert five grains of incense; the candle burns at Masses through the Easter season and at baptisms and funerals through the year.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the word apocalypse: not destruction, but an unveiling. Your line was an unveiling. Did something look different once you asked what was behind it? Day six hundred twenty.

It's the dark of Holy Saturday night. Outside a church, a fire is crackling, and a priest holds a tall new candle, the paschal candle, which will stand near the altar all through the Easter season. Following the rite, he may trace a cross into the wax with a stylus. Above the cross, a Greek letter, alpha. Below it, another, omega. Then the four numbers of the current year, one in each corner of the cross. He presses in five grains of incense for the wounds of Christ, and lights it from the fire. The letters he just carved come from the first chapter of the Apocalypse.
screen: `FIRE ON HOLY SATURDAY NIGHT.` → `ALPHA, OMEGA, THIS YEAR.` → `FROM APOCALYPSE ONE.`

segments.voice: Early in the book, God speaks. In the Douay-Rheims: "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, saith the Lord God, who is, and who was, and who is to come, the Almighty." Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, omega the last. We'd say A to Z. And A to Z doesn't just mean the two ends. It means every letter in between. Every word that could ever be spelled. Then John tells us where he is: on the island of Patmos, for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus. On the Lord's day he hears a voice behind him like a trumpet. He turns around and sees seven golden candlesticks, and among them one like the Son of man. White hair like wool. Eyes like a flame. A voice like many waters. A face shining like the sun. John does what anyone would do. He falls at his feet like a dead man. And then the figure lays his right hand on him. "Fear not. I am the First and the Last." He goes on: I was dead, and now I'm alive forever, and I hold the keys of death. Notice the title. In Isaiah, the first and the last is what God calls himself. Here the risen Christ says it. That's why the priest carves those letters into the Easter candle, saying that all time belongs to Christ, and the ages too. The year we're living in goes on the same wax. Whatever happens between this year's first page and its last, it's inside his A to Z.
screen: `A TO Z, AND EVERYTHING BETWEEN.` · `A VOICE BEHIND HIM ON PATMOS.` · `HE FALLS; A HAND LAID ON HIM.` · `THE YEAR CARVED ON THE CANDLE.` · then, large: `I AM ALPHA AND OMEGA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trace A and Omega. With a fingertip, on your palm, a table, or your knee, slowly trace a capital A. Breathe in as you draw it. Then trace an omega, a horseshoe shape with little feet, like an upside-down U. Breathe out as you draw it. Do it again, slowly. Then let the space between your two letters hold your day so far, and whatever's left of it: the beginning, the end, and everything in the middle. If you pray, you can rest in the line, I am the First and the Last. If you don't, just keep tracing and breathing. The bell holds the time.
Patmos, the island. Where John received the vision of the Apocalypse, including Christ's words: I am Alpha and Omega, the first and the last. Today's word.
Your line: the first and the last. Today, at the start of something and again at its end, trace the two letters with your thumb. Day six hundred twenty.

621.title: Thy first charity (Apocalypse 2:1–7)
621.hook: Ephesus works hard but has left its first love
621.howItsDone: Catholics may return to their first love for God through retreats, renewing baptismal promises at Easter, going back to confession, or revisiting the prayers and practices that first drew them into faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patmos carved into the Easter candle. Your line was the first and the last. Did you trace the two letters at a beginning and an end? Day six hundred twenty-one.

They run their home like a well-managed company. A shared calendar. The bills paid on time. The kids at practice, the groceries ordered, the car serviced. Nothing is falling apart. Ask either of them and they'd say things are fine. And they are fine. It's just that neither can remember the last time they sat on the porch and simply talked, the way they did when they first met, for hours, about nothing. After the vision of chapter one, the Apocalypse turns to seven short letters for seven churches. The first goes to Ephesus. It's a letter to a very well-run church.
screen: `A HOME RUN LIKE A COMPANY.` → `NOTHING FALLING APART.` → `A LETTER TO EPHESUS.`

segments.voice: Ephesus was a great city, home to the temple of the goddess the Douay-Rheims calls Diana, Artemis in Greek. Paul had spent years there, the Acts of the Apostles says. Christian tradition says John lived there too, and some traditions add Mary. This was a church with history. And the letter opens with praise. I know your works, Christ says. Your labor, your patience. You can't stand evil. You've tested people who called themselves apostles and found them false. You've endured, for my name, and haven't grown weary. Then the turn. In the Douay-Rheims: "But I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first charity." First charity: your first love. Everything is working except the thing everything was for. The works are there. The love that started them has drifted away, the way a couple can keep a house running and stop really seeing each other. The remedy comes in three steps. Remember where you fell from. Repent, which the Douay-Rheims calls doing penance. And do the first works, the things you did when the love was new. Not new strategies. The first things. The warning is serious: otherwise, he says, I will move your candlestick out of its place. A church can stay busy and still go out like a lamp. But the letter ends with a promise, as every one of the seven does: to him that overcometh, I will give to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God. The tree from the garden of Eden, closed off since Genesis, opens again at the end of the Bible.
screen: `EPHESUS: A CHURCH WITH HISTORY.` · `I KNOW THY WORKS.` · `THOU HAST LEFT THY FIRST CHARITY.` · `REMEMBER, REPENT, DO THE FIRST WORKS.` · then, large: `THE TREE OF LIFE, OPEN AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember your first love for God. Sit comfortably and breathe. Go back, as far as you need to, to a time when faith felt alive to you: a first Communion, a retreat, a moment in an empty church, a prayer that was answered, or simply a time you felt close to God. If you've never had a moment like that, think of the first time anything stirred your sense of wonder: a night sky, a piece of music. Let the memory come back in detail. What did you do then that you've stopped doing? If you pray, you can ask for that first love back. The bell holds the time.
Ephesus, the city. The first of the seven churches addressed in Apocalypse two, praised for its labor but told it had left its first love. Today's word.
Your line: the first charity. Today, do one of the first works again, the thing you did when the love was new. Day six hundred twenty-one.

622.title: Lukewarm (Apocalypse 3:14–22)
622.tomorrow: I stand at the gate and knock
622.howItsDone: Catholic spiritual writers have long warned against lukewarmness, or spiritual sloth, and Catholics often fight it with small, regular commitments: a daily prayer time, weekly Mass, a monthly confession, done wholeheartedly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephesus, busy and faithful, but missing its first love. Your line was the first charity. Which of the first works did you do again? Day six hundred twenty-two.

You order a coffee and take a sip. Not hot. You'd have taken iced coffee happily, cold and sharp. You'd have taken a steaming cup that warms your hands. But this one has been sitting under the lamp too long, and it's neither. You set it down, and you don't pick it up again. Everyone knows the face people make at a lukewarm drink. The last of the seven letters in the Apocalypse uses that face, and it goes to a city that had money, comfort, and, if the historians are right, a water problem.
screen: `A COFFEE, NEITHER HOT NOR COLD.` → `THE FACE EVERYONE MAKES.` → `THE LETTER TO LAODICEA.`

segments.voice: Laodicea was rich. It was a banking town, known for fine wool and for an eye medicine. The Roman historian Tacitus records that when an earthquake struck it in the year sixty, the city rebuilt from its own wealth, without help from Rome. Now listen to Christ's words to its church, in the Douay-Rheims: "I know thy works, that thou art neither cold, nor hot. I would thou wert cold, or hot. But because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold, nor hot, I will begin to vomit thee out of my mouth." That's strong language, the face at the coffee cup. Many scholars point to the city's water. Nearby Hierapolis had famous hot springs, good for healing. Colossae, not far off, had cold, fresh water, good for drinking. Laodicea's water, on this reading, came in through a long aqueduct and arrived tepid. Read that way, hot and cold aren't zealous and hostile. Both are useful: one heals, one refreshes. Lukewarm does neither. And the church's problem matches the city's pride. Thou sayest, I am rich and have need of nothing, the letter goes on, and knowest not that thou art poor, and blind, and naked. Rich, but poor. A city of eye medicine, but blind. A city of wool, but naked. So Christ counsels them to get true gold, white garments and salve for their eyes from him. And then, so the harshness isn't misread: "Such as I love, I rebuke and chastise." This is a rebuke from someone who wants them back. Not a door slammed. The very next verse, tomorrow's, is about a door, and who is standing outside it.
screen: `A RICH CITY THAT REBUILT ITSELF.` · `NEITHER COLD NOR HOT.` · `HOT HEALS, COLD REFRESHES.` · `RICH, BUT POOR, BLIND AND NAKED.` · then, large: `SUCH AS I LOVE, I REBUKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing wholeheartedly. Sit comfortably and breathe. Look at today and find one thing you'd normally do half-there: washing dishes, a walk, a conversation with a child, a prayer, a piece of work. Choose it. Now picture doing it with all of you: phone away, full attention, no rushing toward the next thing. Feel what that would be like in your hands and shoulders. Not more effort, just more presence. If you pray, you can offer that one thing to God, done warmly. If you don't, just commit to it fully in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Lukewarm. Apocalypse three: neither cold nor hot, neither refreshing nor healing, comfortable and half-there. Today's word.
Your line: not lukewarm. Today, do the thing you chose with your whole self, start to finish, even if it's only ten minutes. Day six hundred twenty-two.

fork.reveal: the rebuke is fierce, but the letter says why: such as I love, I rebuke and chastise. and the next verse is a knock at the door.

original.note: Greek: lukewarm, tepid (Apocalypse 3:16), the only time the word appears in the New Testament.

trapdoor: what you thought: lukewarm means not religious enough.
what it means: comfortable, self-satisfied, half-there: neither healing like hot water nor refreshing like cold.
what a scholar hears: Laodicea's tepid aqueduct water, between Hierapolis's hot springs and Colossae's cold water; and Tacitus on its self-funded rebuilding.

623.title: I stand at the gate and knock (Apocalypse 3:20)
623.word: I stand at the gate and knock
623.hook: if any man open the door, I will come in and sup with him
623.howItsDone: Some Catholics pray with this verse in Eucharistic adoration and before Communion, and it is used at retreats and in invitations to return to the sacraments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laodicea and the lukewarm coffee. Your line was not lukewarm. What did you do with your whole self? Day six hundred twenty-three.

In the eighteen-fifties an English painter, William Holman Hunt, painted Christ at night, standing at a door in a dark garden, holding a lantern and knocking. The door is overgrown with weeds and ivy. It hasn't been opened in a long time. Prints of it were hung in homes and churches, and people noticed something odd about it. The door has no handle on the outside. The story goes that when someone pointed this out, Hunt said that was the point: this door can only be opened from within. He took the scene from one verse.
screen: `A LANTERN AT A DARK DOOR.` → `OVERGROWN WITH IVY.` → `NO HANDLE ON THE OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Here it is, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold, I stand at the gate, and knock. If any man shall hear my voice, and open to me the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me." Remember who this is said to. Not to strangers who have never heard of Christ. To Laodicea, the lukewarm church, the one that said it needed nothing. He has just rebuked them, because he loves them, and now he's outside their door, knocking. The Lord of the vision in chapter one, with eyes like flame and keys of death, waits on a doorstep. Notice what he doesn't do. He doesn't break the door down. He doesn't climb in a window. The power is all on the inside: if any man hear, and open. Then notice the promise. Sup with him. The Greek word is the one for supper, the evening meal, the long one at the end of work, where people actually talk. Not a quick visit at the door. A meal at your table. Some readers hear an echo of the Song of Songs, where the beloved knocks at night and calls, open to me. For Catholics the line also points toward the altar, where Christ comes to his people in a meal. And the promise is to any man, any one. The church as a whole may be lukewarm. One person can still open. In the Douay-Rheims the verse has gate and door both. Holman Hunt painted the door overgrown, a door that hadn't moved in years. That doesn't seem to discourage the one knocking.
screen: `SAID TO THE LUKEWARM CHURCH.` · `HE DOESN'T BREAK THE DOOR DOWN.` · `SUP: THE LONG EVENING MEAL.` · `ANY ONE PERSON CAN OPEN.` · then, large: `BEHOLD, I STAND AT THE GATE, AND KNOCK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open a door as a prayer. If there's a door near you, go and stand by it. If not, picture one: your front door, your bedroom door. Put your hand on the handle. Breathe. Think of a part of your life that's been closed for a while, overgrown: a grief, a habit, a relationship, a question about God you stopped asking. Then slowly open the door, all the way, and leave it open for a few breaths. Feel the air move. If you pray, you can let the opening be your prayer, without words. If you don't, just notice what it's like to open something on purpose. The bell holds the time.
I stand at the gate and knock. Apocalypse three: Christ waits outside, and the door opens from the inside. Today's word.
screen: `I STAND AT THE GATE AND KNOCK — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: I stand and knock. Today, every time you open a door, let it remind you of the one knocking. And that's week eighty-nine: love the one you see, able to keep you, an unveiling, the first and the last, the first charity, not lukewarm, and I stand and knock. Day six hundred twenty-three.

original.note: Greek: I will sup, eat the evening meal (Apocalypse 3:20), from deipnon, supper.

trapdoor: what you thought: a gentle invitation to people outside the Church.
what it means: Christ knocking on the door of his own lukewarm church, waiting to be let in for a real meal together.
